evidence: Traupman 62: ē lectō surgere, to get out of bed

terms.gloss: rise up, get to one’s feet
evidence: Traupman 57: nōn omnīnō cōnsurgere possum, I can’t get up at all
terms.comment: Rising together or rising all the way up, as from a seat or the ground.

terms.gloss: stand up for someone, rise out of respect
terms.grammar: with the dative of the person
evidence: Cic. Pis. 12: an quisquam in cūriam venientī adsurrēxit? (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 34: stand up (as a mark of respect), assurge (assurgite)

phrases.english: get up and walk: Dad, lifting the sleeping boy out of bed (Mt 9, 5, in jest)

sources: Lewis & Short: surgo · Dickinson: Latin Core Vocabulary

Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 7 November 2026, with their glosses. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word; classical passages are cited by author.
The example sentences marked “composed” are ours.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
